b41.content:
Written by an Anglican clergyman’s son who became a Catholic priest, this early dystopian novel imagines a secular world government and a charismatic leader who wins the world’s allegiance, while a persecuted Church dwindles around the pope.

Popes Benedict XVI and Francis both recommended it for its prophetic insight.

b42.content:
A French Trappist abbot’s warning that active ministry without an interior life of prayer becomes empty. He argues that all fruitful apostolic work must flow from union with Christ.

Pope St. Pius X kept it by his bedside, and it has been essential reading for priests and lay apostles ever since.

b43.content:
Chesterton’s sweeping retelling of human history, written partly in response to H.G. Wells, argues that humanity is unique among creatures and that Christ is unique among religious figures.

C.S. Lewis credited it with helping him move toward Christianity.

b44.content:
Told through the journal of a young, sickly priest in a rural French parish, the novel portrays his struggles with a hostile and indifferent congregation and his own sense of failure.

It ends with the famous words "Grace is everywhere," and was made into a celebrated film by Robert Bresson.

b45.content:
Set during the anti-Catholic persecution in 1930s Mexico, Greene’s novel follows an unnamed "whisky priest," deeply flawed, who continues to administer the sacraments while fleeing a police lieutenant determined to wipe out religion.

It is a powerful story about grace working through human weakness.

b46.content:
Charles Ryder recalls his entanglement with the aristocratic Catholic Flyte family, from his Oxford friendship with Sebastian Flyte through the decline of their great house. Waugh described its theme as "the operation of divine grace" on a varied group of characters.

It is one of the best-known Catholic novels of the twentieth century.

b47.content:
The German Thomist philosopher argues that true leisure is not idleness but a receptive, contemplative attitude toward reality, and that it is rooted in worship.

Without the celebration of divine worship, he warns, a culture reduced to "total work" loses its soul.

b48.content:
The autobiography of the journalist and activist who co-founded the Catholic Worker movement with Peter Maurin. Day recounts her radical youth, the birth of her daughter, her conversion, and her life of voluntary poverty serving the homeless.

Her cause for canonization is open, and she is honored as a Servant of God.

b49.content:
Sheen’s long meditation on the life of Jesus emphasizes that Christ, unlike any other person, came into the world in order to die. It reflects on the Gospel events with theological depth and vivid, accessible prose.

It remains the best-known book by the famous preacher and television host.

b50.content:
O’Connor’s first story collection, set in the American South, is known for its dark humor and sudden violence. Her characters often meet grace in shocking and unwelcome forms.

A devout Catholic, O’Connor wrote that her subject was "the action of grace in territory held largely by the devil."

b51.content:
The sixteen documents of Vatican II include four constitutions: on the liturgy (Sacrosanctum Concilium), the Church (Lumen Gentium), divine revelation (Dei Verbum), and the Church in the modern world (Gaudium et Spes).

They continue to shape Catholic life, worship, and dialogue worldwide.

b52.content:
Based on lectures the young theologian gave at Tübingen, this book works through the Apostles’ Creed to explain what it means to believe in a skeptical modern age.

It remains one of the most widely read works of twentieth-century theology.

b53.content:
An American Jesuit who secretly entered the Soviet Union, Ciszek spent twenty-three years in Soviet prisons and Siberian labor camps. This book reflects on the spiritual lessons of those years.

Its theme is total abandonment to God’s will in every circumstance. His cause for canonization is open.

b54.content:
A series of 129 catechetical addresses given at weekly general audiences. John Paul II reflects on the meaning of the human body, sexuality, and marriage in light of creation, the Fall, and redemption.

It has had wide influence on Catholic teaching about marriage and the human person.

b55.content:
The official summary of Catholic belief and practice, organized in four parts: the profession of faith, the celebration of the Christian mystery (the sacraments), life in Christ (morality), and Christian prayer.

Its extensive references to Scripture, councils, and saints make it a guide to the whole tradition.

b56.content:
An encyclical on the relationship between faith and reason, which opens by comparing them to "two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth."

It calls philosophers to recover confidence in reason’s ability to reach truth, and theologians to engage seriously with philosophy.

b57.content:
A contemporary French priest explains that true freedom is found not in controlling circumstances but in faith, hope, and love, which let us accept what we cannot change and live fully in the present.

Its short chapters are gentle, practical, and widely loved.

b58.content:
A three-volume study of the life of Jesus, from the infancy narratives through the Baptism and public ministry to the Passion and Resurrection. Benedict wrote it as a personal work, drawing on both historical scholarship and faith.

He sought to show that the Jesus of the Gospels is the real, historical Jesus.

b59.content:
Pope Francis’s first apostolic exhortation calls for a missionary Church that goes out to the peripheries, marked by the joy of the Gospel. It addresses preaching, the poor, and the pastoral conversion of parishes and structures.

It served as a programmatic document for his pontificate.

b60.content:
An encyclical "on care for our common home," named for the refrain of St. Francis’s Canticle of the Creatures. It links care for the environment with care for the poor and critiques consumerism and the "throwaway culture."

It proposes an "integral ecology" in which everything is connected.

b61.content:
Written as a prayerful meditation, the Proslogion seeks a single argument that would show God exists. Anselm finds it in the idea of God as the greatest conceivable being, the famous "ontological argument."

Philosophers from Aquinas to Kant to the present have debated it, but the book begins and ends as a prayer of faith seeking understanding.

b62.content:
A short treatise answering two questions: why God should be loved, and how much. Bernard traces four degrees of love, from loving oneself for one’s own sake to loving oneself only for God’s sake.

It is one of the gems of medieval spiritual writing, both theological and deeply personal.

b63.content:
Written on Mount La Verna, where St. Francis received the stigmata, this short work describes six stages by which the soul rises to God: through the created world, through its own powers, and finally beyond all understanding into loving union.

It is a masterpiece of Franciscan spirituality and medieval theology.

b64.content:
An English Augustinian canon’s guide to the contemplative life, written for an anchoress. Hilton describes the soul’s reform from sin to the restored image of God, and warns against seeking extraordinary experiences.

It was one of the most widely read spiritual books in England before the Reformation.

b65.content:
More’s witty dialogue describes a traveler’s account of an island commonwealth with no private property, religious tolerance, and communal life. It gave the English language the word "utopia," meaning both "good place" and "no place."

Scholars still debate how seriously More meant its ideas, which satirize the injustices of his own Europe.

b66.content:
Written in the Tower of London while More awaited execution, this dialogue between an old Hungarian and his nephew, facing a Turkish invasion, reflects on how a Christian should meet persecution and death.

Through its fictional setting, More prepares himself and his readers to stand firm with good humor and trust in God.

b67.content:
Teresa’s autobiography, written at the command of her confessors, recounts her lukewarm early years in the convent, her conversion, and the mystical graces that followed. At its center is a treatise on prayer comparing the soul to a garden watered in four ways.

It is one of the great spiritual autobiographies, honest and often funny.

b68.content:
A companion to Dark Night of the Soul, the Ascent is a demanding guide to the "active" purification of the senses and spirit through detachment from everything that is not God.

Its sketch of the mountain, with the word "nothing" repeated along the narrow path to the summit, is one of the most famous images in Christian mysticism.

b69.content:
Near the end of his life, Ignatius dictated this account of his conversion to a fellow Jesuit. It covers his wounding at Pamplona, his conversion while convalescing, his time at Manresa, and his pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

Ignatius refers to himself throughout as "the pilgrim," and the book shows the Spiritual Exercises taking shape in his own life.

b70.content:
Commissioned by the Council of Trent and published under Pope St. Pius V, this catechism was written for parish priests to use in teaching. It covers the Creed, the sacraments, the Ten Commandments, and the Lord’s Prayer.

It remained the Church’s authoritative catechism for four centuries, until the Catechism of the Catholic Church in 1992.

b71.content:
A collection of fifty-two short chapters, or "roses," explaining the history, power, and method of praying the Rosary, with stories of its fruits and practical advice for praying it well.

It remains one of the most popular books on the Rosary.

b72.content:
A book of meditations on death, judgment, and eternity. Alphonsus wrote it to move sinners to conversion and to help the faithful live each day in light of eternity.

Its plain, urgent style made it one of the most widely read devotional books of the 18th and 19th centuries.

b73.content:
Written as Newman was deciding whether to become Catholic, this essay argues that Christian doctrine grows over time like a living idea, unfolding its implications without changing its essence. He proposes tests for telling true development from corruption.

Newman was received into the Catholic Church before he finished it. It deeply influenced later theology, including the Second Vatican Council.

b74.content:
Lectures Newman gave as founding rector of the Catholic University of Ireland. He argues that a university should cultivate a "liberal education" of the whole mind, with theology among the sciences, rather than training only for a profession.

It remains a classic of educational philosophy.

b75.content:
A long dramatic poem following the soul of a dying old man, Gerontius, from his deathbed through judgment to purgatory, accompanied by his guardian angel. It includes the hymn "Praise to the Holiest in the Height."

Edward Elgar set it to music in 1900 in one of the great English choral works.

b76.content:
Written by a poet who had lived in poverty and opium addiction on the streets of London, this ode describes a soul fleeing God, who pursues it relentlessly like a hound.

It is one of the most famous religious poems in English.

b77.content:
Set in Nero’s Rome, this historical novel follows the love of a Roman officer, Marcus Vinicius, for Lygia, a young Christian, amid the great fire and the persecution that followed. Sts. Peter and Paul appear among the characters.

The title recalls the legend of Peter meeting Christ on the Appian Way. It helped win Sienkiewicz the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1905.

b78.content:
The first collection of detective stories featuring Father Brown, a small, unassuming Catholic priest who solves crimes through his deep understanding of human nature and sin, learned in the confessional.

The stories are clever puzzles and quiet meditations on reason, grace, and mercy.

b79.content:
A short, influential book by the Italian-German priest Romano Guardini on the nature of Catholic worship. Guardini describes the liturgy as "play" before God: done not for any purpose but for its own sake, in the presence of the Father.

It helped inspire the liturgical movement of the 20th century. Joseph Ratzinger later wrote a book with the same title in tribute.

b80.content:
Hopkins, an English Jesuit priest, wrote startlingly original poems about the glory of God in nature, such as "God’s Grandeur," "Pied Beauty," and "The Windhover." They were published by his friend Robert Bridges nearly thirty years after his death.

His innovative "sprung rhythm" made him one of the most influential poets of the modern age.
